questions.question: Define globalisation with its practical test, then explain its causes using the two-family structure with one fully worked mechanism per family.
questions.expected_answer: Globalisation is the process through which the world's economies grow increasingly interconnected and interdependent — goods, services, capital, workers and information crossing borders until national economies operate as components of one world system; the practical test is that an event on one continent moves prices, jobs and incomes on another within weeks. Technology family (made it possible): the standardised shipping container is packed once and craned from vessel to rail to road without opening, which collapsed freight costs, which made manufacturing far from customers profitable — enabling global value chains coordinated in real time over undersea cables and the internet. Policy family (made it permitted): tariffs were negotiated down round after round, culminating in the WTO in 1995; exchange controls were dismantled so finance moves at a keystroke; and closed economies — China from 1978, the Soviet bloc after 1989, South Africa after 1994 — rejoined the world market.

questions.question: Set out globalisation's two-sided scorecard for South Africa — two gains and two losses with evidence — and state the balanced verdict.
questions.expected_answer: Gains: world-scale vehicle plants at Kariega, East London and Rosslyn built by foreign investment, sustaining over one hundred thousand jobs across assembly and components; lower consumer prices and wider choice — cheap imports acting like an unannounced pay rise; plus faster technology diffusion and foreign capital covering our savings shortfall. Losses: textile and footwear centres in KwaZulu-Natal and the Western Cape hollowed out when tariffs fell, costing tens of thousands of jobs; contagion — the 2008 crisis began in American housing finance yet cut around a million South African jobs in the downturn because our customers stopped ordering; plus a thinning tax base as mobile multinationals shift profits, and widening internal inequality. Verdict: globalisation grows the total and moves the shares, so policy must harvest the gains while re-skilling and shielding those the losses fall on — never a simple for-or-against.

questions.question: Explain the North/South divide through its three mechanisms, using the chocolate bar, and name two forces reshaping the divide.
questions.expected_answer: The divide is the persistent economic gap between the developed North and the developing South — shorthand about wealth, not latitude. Mechanism one, terms of trade: cocoa grows in Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire and sells raw for cents, while roasting, branding and retail in Europe capture the thirty-rand slab price; selling raw and buying made is a treadmill, since raw prices swing and buy fewer machines over time. Mechanism two, debt: Southern countries borrow in dollars, so Northern rate rises or currency slips balloon repayments until schools and clinics are trimmed. Mechanism three, voice: the IMF, World Bank and WTO rulebooks were drafted where Northern votes dominated — visible in tariffs that stay low on raw cocoa and climb on chocolate. Reshaping forces: China and India dragging the world's economic centre southward; BRICS (South Africa included) demanding a Southern voice; and the AfCFTA building Africa's internal market so the finishing stays in Africa.
